PART 1: NARRATION READY
Let's talk about transformer PL1M. This unit is operating in a tuned-field environment — meaning your team has already made the investment in MPTS correction, the assets are in the field, and the electromagnetic correction architecture is live. That's the right starting point. You're not at square one. Here's where we stand for this analysis cycle, though. The data we need to do a full numeric review — the Mercury CSV file and the capture images for PL1M — weren't available when this session ran. That means power factor is value unavailable. Peak demand is value unavailable. Reactive load in kVAR is value unavailable. The daily supply target in kVA is value unavailable. What that tells us is not that the transformer is in trouble — it tells us we have an open diagnostic item that needs to be closed. In a tuned field, the question we're always asking is: how well is the current correction holding, and how much optimization gap is still sitting there? The difference between your TBT anchor — where the field is today — and your TS projection — where it could go with refined tuning — that delta represents real recoverable savings and real heat burden relief. We just can't quantify it yet for PL1M. So the action here is clear: get that data submitted, get the images into the system, and let's put numbers on the optimization gap. Once we have TBT and TS aligned for PL1M, we'll know exactly how much power factor improvement is still available, how much thermal burden can still be reduced, and whether the installed assets are sized correctly for this transformer's current load reality. PL1M is flagged as a gap item in this site review. It travels into the group overview with that flag clearly attached. ---

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
For transformer PL1M — this unit is in a tuned field. Prior MPTS investment is live. That's already a win. But this analysis cycle ran without data. No Mercury CSV, no capture images. Power factor, reactive load, voltage stability, thermal burden — all value unavailable. We can't quantify the optimization gap between TBT and TS without those numbers. And that gap is where the remaining savings live — the recoverable energy, the heat burden reduction, the final push toward a 99.5% power factor target. The action is straightforward: resubmit PL1M's data. Get the TBT, TV, TM, and TS views into the system. Verify that the installed MPTS hardware is holding correction without drift. It doesn't stop the group site overview from running — but it absolutely needs to be resolved before any site-level conclusions are considered complete. ---

PART 3: ENGINEERING DETAILED
Let me walk you through the full picture on transformer PL1M, and I want to be direct with you about what we know and what we don't. PL1M is a tuned-field transformer. That means your organization has already committed capital to MPTS correction on this unit. The equipment is installed, the correction is in operation, and the electromagnetic field on this transformer is not in a raw, uncorrected state. That prior investment is real, and it matters. Tuned fields deliver lower reactive burden, reduced thermal stress, and improved power factor compared to where you started — and those gains compound over time in equipment longevity and operating cost. Now, here is the challenge for this analysis cycle. When our session ran for PL1M, neither the Mercury CSV data nor the visual capture images were available. That means every numeric anchor we would normally extract — power factor at the TBT view, kVAR maximum, kVAR average, peak demand in kilowatts, daily supply target in kVA, thermal burden in BTU per hour, cooling overhead in dollars per hour — all of those are value unavailable. We ran the extraction framework, the framework found nothing to extract, and I want to be transparent about that rather than fill in estimated numbers that aren't grounded in evidence. What this means in the tuned-field optimization context is specific. We use the TBT view as our anchor — it shows us the field as it currently exists, post-installation, in its corrected-but-still-improvable state. We then look at the TS view to understand the projected outcome of incremental optimization: how much power factor improvement remains, how much reactive energy can still be recovered, how much heat burden can still be moved off the transformer, and what the annual dollar value of that remaining gap represents. The spread between TBT and TS is the optimization opportunity — and for most tuned transformers, it's meaningful. Power factor typically moves from wherever TBT anchors it toward the 99.5% TS target. Thermal burden drops measurably. Cooling overhead decreases. Annual savings from closing that gap can be substantial depending on the transformer's reactive load profile. For PL1M, none of that can be quantified today. We also could not run the voltage stability review from the TV view — so dip event frequency, proximity to the 480-volt nominal reference, and outage event detection from gold-streak analysis are all unconfirmed. We could not evaluate harmonic content from the TM view, which matters particularly if PL1M serves variable-frequency drive loads, large motor starts, or other nonlinear equipment common in food processing and rendering environments. Here is what I recommend. First, resubmit the PL1M data — the Mercury CSV and the TBT, TV, TM, and TS capture images — as soon as possible. Second, while that data is being gathered, have a field technician verify that the installed MPTS assets on PL1M are operating correctly. Correction drift can happen over time — capacitor bank degradation, control system issues, connection changes — and it doesn't always announce itself with an obvious alarm. A physical inspection of the correction hardware is appropriate, particularly if it's been more than six months since the last verification. Third, when the reactive data comes in, confirm that the kVAR compensation capacity installed on PL1M is still correctly matched to the transformer's current load profile. Industrial loads grow and shift — and if throughput has increased or equipment has been added since the original sizing was done, the installed assets may be undercompensating. PL1M carries a data-gap flag into the group site overview for this review cycle. It does not prevent us from synthesizing the other transformers — but it is a gap that must be closed before we can deliver a complete site-level conclusion with confidence. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard. ---
